description: Interviews, questionnaires, case studies, observations, correlation and scatter diagrams.
content_html:
Beyond the Experiment

Experiments are powerful tools for establishing causation, but they are not always possible or appropriate. Some questions in psychology cannot be answered experimentally — it would be unethical to manipulate certain variables, or the topic is too complex to reduce to a single controlled setting. For these situations, psychologists use non-experimental methods: interviews, questionnaires, case studies and observation studies. Each has its own strengths and weaknesses, and each is suited to different kinds of research questions.

Quantitative and Qualitative Methods

Non-experimental methods can produce either quantitative data (numerical results, such as scores, frequencies or percentages) or qualitative data (detailed descriptions of experience, such as what participants say or how they behave). Most methods can produce either, depending on how they are used — a questionnaire can include both numerical rating scales (quantitative) and open-ended questions inviting longer responses (qualitative).

An interview involves a researcher asking questions and recording the participant’s responses. Interviews can be structured (every participant asked the same predetermined questions in the same order, producing quantitative data) or unstructured (open conversation following the participant’s responses, producing rich qualitative data).

Strength of interviews: they can explore complex experiences in depth; unstructured interviews allow unexpected themes to emerge. Weakness: interviewer bias — the researcher’s manner, appearance or phrasing can influence participant responses; time-consuming and difficult to analyse consistently, especially unstructured data.

A questionnaire is a set of written questions completed by participants, often without the researcher present. Questions can be closed (ticking a box, rating on a scale — produces quantitative data) or open (written response — produces qualitative data).

Strength: large numbers of participants can be reached cheaply and quickly; no interviewer bias if completed independently; easy to analyse if questions are closed. Weakness: participants may not answer honestly (social desirability bias — giving the answer they think they should give rather than their true answer); ambiguous questions can be interpreted differently; low response rates may produce a biased sample.

A case study is an in-depth investigation of a single individual, group or event. It typically uses a combination of methods (interviews, observation, psychometric tests) to build a detailed picture of the case. Case studies are particularly useful when the case is unusual or extreme — for example, studying an individual with a rare neurological condition to understand normal brain function by contrast.

Strength: provides rich, detailed qualitative data that captures complexity; unique cases can generate hypotheses for further research; can study variables that could not be manipulated experimentally. Weakness: findings cannot be generalised to other people because the case may be unique; the researcher may develop a subjective attachment to the participant; results are not replicable.

In an observation study, the researcher watches and records participants’ behaviour without manipulating any variables. Observations can be naturalistic (watching behaviour in its natural setting) or structured (in a controlled setting with predetermined categories to record).

A key technical requirement of observation studies is using categories of behaviour — a predetermined list of specific, clearly defined behaviours to record (e.g. ‘number of times participant initiates conversation’ rather than ‘social behaviour’). This makes data more objective and consistent.

Interobserver reliability is a crucial check: two or more observers independently record the same behaviour, and their records are compared. High agreement indicates the observation categories are clear and consistently applicable. Strength: naturalistic observations have high ecological validity. Weakness: observer bias — what one person notices may differ from another; participants who know they are being watched may behave differently (Hawthorne effect).

Correlation

A correlation measures the association between two variables. It tells us whether, as one variable increases, the other tends to increase (positive correlation), decrease (negative correlation) or show no consistent pattern (no correlation).

Correlations are displayed using scatter diagrams. Each participant provides two scores (one for each variable), which are plotted as a single dot on the graph. A positive correlation produces dots trending from bottom-left to top-right. A negative correlation produces dots trending from top-left to bottom-right. A weak or no correlation produces a scattered cluster with no clear trend.

Key Fact

A correlation shows association, not causation. Two variables may be strongly correlated because a third, unmeasured variable causes both. This is called a third variable problem. For example, ice cream sales and drowning rates both increase in summer, but ice cream does not cause drowning — hot weather (the third variable) drives both.

Strengths and Weaknesses of Correlations

Strength: correlations allow researchers to study the relationship between variables that cannot be manipulated ethically (e.g. the association between stress and illness). They are also useful as a starting point for identifying patterns that may be worth investigating with a controlled experiment.

Weakness: correlations cannot establish causation. Because neither variable is manipulated, we cannot conclude that one variable causes the other. This is the most important limitation of correlational research.

Key Fact

Non-experimental methods summary: interviews (verbal, structured or unstructured), questionnaires (written, closed or open), case studies (in-depth single case), observations (behaviour categories, interobserver reliability checked). None of these establish causation — only a controlled experiment can do that.
exam_tip_html: The key distinction examiners test in research methods is whether a method produces quantitative or qualitative data, and whether it establishes causation. Remember: non-experimental methods (interviews, questionnaires, observations, correlations) do not establish causation — only experiments with controlled manipulation of the IV can do that. For correlation questions, always state specifically that a correlation cannot prove causation, and explain the third variable problem for full marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Non-experimental methods include interviews (verbal, can be structured/unstructured), questionnaires (written, closed or open questions), case studies (in-depth single case) and observations (watching behaviour, using categories, checked by interobserver reliability).
  • Correlations measure the association between two variables and are displayed on scatter diagrams; they do not establish causation because a third variable may explain the relationship.
  • Quantitative data is numerical; qualitative data is in words. Most research methods can produce either type depending on how questions are framed.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes interobserver reliability?
A) When the same researcher gets the same results on two separate occasions
B) When two or more independent observers record the same behaviours consistently
C) When a questionnaire is completed twice by the same participant
D) When experimental results can be replicated in a different laboratory
practice_questions.marks: B) When two or more independent observers record the same behaviours consistently [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define what is meant by 'qualitative data'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'Data expressed in words or descriptions rather than numbers, providing rich detail about experiences, feelings or opinions.' — both elements present and clearly linked.
Secure: Correct core idea — data in words and reference to detail or experience.
Developing: Mentions 'words' but without contrasting with numerical or quantitative data.
Emerging: Incorrect or incomplete definition.

practice_questions.text: Describe one strength and one weakness of using a questionnaire in psychological research.
practice_questions.marks:
Strength: large numbers of participants can be reached quickly and cheaply; no interviewer bias if completed independently.
Weakness: social desirability bias — participants may not answer honestly, giving responses they believe are expected rather than true answers.
Mastering: Both clearly described with developed reason.
Secure: Both identified, one developed.
Developing: One point explained.
Emerging: One vague point.

practice_questions.text: A researcher finds a positive correlation between the number of hours students spend on social media and their reported levels of anxiety. Explain what this correlation tells us and what it does not tell us.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should:
- State that a positive correlation means as social media use increases, anxiety also tends to increase (the two variables move in the same direction).
- Explain that the correlation does not tell us that social media use causes anxiety.
- Explain the third variable problem: a third variable (e.g. pre-existing stress, personality) may cause both increased social media use and increased anxiety.
- Conclude: only a controlled experiment can establish causation.
Mastering: Direction of correlation, causation limitation, third variable explanation all clear.
Secure: Causation limitation stated, third variable mentioned.
Developing: Causation limitation stated without development.
Emerging: Describes what a correlation is without addressing causation.

practice_questions.text: Describe the key features of an observation study, including the use of categories of behaviour and interobserver reliability.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should cover:
- Definition: the researcher watches and records behaviour without manipulating variables.
- Can be naturalistic (natural setting) or structured (controlled setting).
- Categories of behaviour: predetermined, clearly defined behaviours to record — makes data objective and consistent.
- Interobserver reliability: two or more observers independently record the same behaviour; their records are compared — high agreement indicates categories are clear and consistently applicable.
- Strength: ecological validity (naturalistic). Weakness: observer bias; Hawthorne effect if participants know they are being watched.
Mastering: All five elements described accurately.
Secure: Four elements present.
Developing: Two or three elements.
Emerging: General description only.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate two non-experimental research methods used in psychology.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1) — any two of interviews, questionnaires, case studies, observation:
- Interview: researcher asks questions; can be structured or unstructured; produces quantitative or qualitative data.
- Questionnaire: written questions; closed (quantitative) or open (qualitative) questions; can reach large samples.
- Case study: in-depth study of single individual; uses multiple methods; rich qualitative data.
- Observation: researcher watches behaviour using predetermined categories; interobserver reliability checked.

Evaluation (AO3) of chosen two methods:
- Interview: strength = depth of data. Weakness = interviewer bias, time-consuming.
- Questionnaire: strength = large samples, cheap. Weakness = social desirability bias, low response rate may bias sample.
- Case study: strength = rich detail, unique cases. Weakness = cannot generalise, subjective.
- Observation: strength = ecological validity (naturalistic). Weakness = observer bias, Hawthorne effect.

Mastering: Two methods described accurately, with two elaborated evaluation points each.
Secure: Two methods described, evaluation for each.
Developing: Two methods described, limited evaluation.
Emerging: One method described.

knowledge_checks.q: What does a scatter diagram display in a correlational study?
options: The mean scores for each condition in an experiment
Each participant's scores on two variables plotted as a single dot
The frequency of behaviours recorded in an observation
The number of participants in each sampling group

knowledge_checks.q: What is social desirability bias in questionnaire research?
options: When participants give answers they think are socially acceptable rather than truthful
When participants are observed behaving differently because they know they are being watched

knowledge_checks.q: In an observation study, _____ reliability is checked by having two observers independently record the same behaviours and comparing their records.
A correlation can tell us about the _____ between two variables but cannot prove that one causes the other.
Match each research method to its key feature:
right: In-depth study of a single individual or group
Researcher watches behaviour using predetermined categories

flashcard_questions.a: Data expressed as numbers, allowing statistical comparison and analysis.
Data expressed in words or descriptions, providing rich detail about experiences.
When participants give responses they think are expected or acceptable rather than truthful answers.
An in-depth study of a single individual, group or event, often using multiple methods.

flashcard_questions.q: What is one strength of a case study?
flashcard_questions.a: Provides rich, detailed data about complex or unusual cases that other methods cannot capture.

flashcard_questions.q: What is one weakness of a case study?
flashcard_questions.a: Findings cannot be generalised to other people because the case may be unique.

flashcard_questions.q: What are categories of behaviour in an observation study?
flashcard_questions.a: Predetermined, clearly defined behaviours the observer records, ensuring consistency.
The degree to which two independent observers record the same behaviours consistently.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a positive correlation on a scatter diagram look like?
flashcard_questions.a: Dots trending from bottom-left to top-right — as one variable increases, so does the other.

flashcard_questions.q: Why can a correlation not prove causation?
flashcard_questions.a: A third variable may cause both variables, creating an association without a direct causal link.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the third variable problem in correlational research?
flashcard_questions.a: When an unmeasured third variable causes both correlated variables, rather than one causing the other.

flashcard_questions.q: What is one strength of using a questionnaire over an interview?
flashcard_questions.a: Questionnaires can reach large numbers of participants quickly and cheaply.

glossary_terms.definition: Data expressed as numbers, allowing for statistical analysis and comparison between groups.
Data expressed in words or descriptions rather than numbers, providing rich detail about experiences and meaning.
A research method in which participants answer questions from a researcher in a verbal, face-to-face or recorded format.
A research method involving a set of written questions completed by participants without a researcher being present.
An in-depth study of a single individual, group or event, often used when the case is unusual or extreme.
A research method in which the researcher watches and records behaviour without directly manipulating any variables.
Clearly defined, mutually exclusive categories for recording behaviour during an observation, used to ensure consistency between observers.
The extent to which two or more observers independently record the same behaviours when observing the same event, used to check consistency of observation categories.
A statistical technique that measures the strength and direction of the association between two variables, without implying that one causes the other.
A graph on which each participant's scores on two variables are plotted as a single dot, used to display the direction and strength of a correlation.
An alternative explanation for a correlation, in which a third variable causes both of the correlated variables rather than one causing the other.

hero_image_caption: Psychologists use interviews, observations and surveys to study behaviour in depth.
